headline: 2 of 6 protein(s) pass every design rule for the lanmodulin architecture, the fold that binds lanthanides. 16 deposited metal site(s) were measured across them, 12 of them holding La3+.
question: what proteins should I try for capturing La3+

caveats: These rules select for the lanmodulin architecture -- four tightly spaced EF-hand loops in a short protein. They are not an affinity, not a selectivity over calcium, and not specific to any one lanthanide: the same rules fire for all fifteen trivalent lanthanides because sequence cannot separate them. Telling two lanthanides apart needs ionic radius against a coordination number measured from structure.

The shortlist does not depend on La3+: every design rule is a lanmodulin-architecture rule and fires identically for all 15 trivalent lanthanides. The ion enters only at the structure step, where it chooses which deposited file to measure and is compared against the geometry found there.

A size match compares one ion's Shannon radius against the mean donor distance actually measured at this site. A good fit says the site is the right size; it is not an affinity, and it does not separate a lanthanide from calcium -- Ca2+ scores above Ce3+ at several real lanthanide sites.

Each site carries `deposited_rank`: where this size score places the ion that was actually crystallised in it, out of the 15 trivalent lanthanides. On this project's own structures that rank is 6th and 9th, not 1st -- the score does not recover the ion known to bind the site. Read the fit as a rough size compatibility, never as a choice between one lanthanide and another.
12 of the 16 deposited metal site(s) measured here hold La3+ and the other 4 hold Nd. Only those 12 are observations of La3+ in a structure; the La3+ fit on the rest is a counterfactual.

The donor distance measured here is a property of this complex, not of the empty protein. An EF-hand loop closes around whichever ion it has: comparing like with like at coordination number 9, the Nd sites of 8FNS average 2.52 A and the Dy sites of 8FNR average 2.43 A, tracking the ionic radii of the two metals. So a low fit for an ion that was not the one crystallised says the loop would have to move, which is what loops do; it is not evidence the protein will not bind that ion.
Threshold is the minimum family median of 4 natural Ln families, fitted and scored on the same points: a descriptive separation, not a validated classifier.
n = 4 families. The claim is the overlap count -- 0 of 55 Ca accessions reach the threshold -- not the p-value, which at this n is mostly a statement about n.
A fifth family may do to coordination number what the fourth did to bidentate carboxylates (ROADMAP 3.19). One descriptor surviving four families is the current state of the evidence, not a result.
Describes an observed coordination geometry. Not an affinity, not a selectivity constant, and not a probability.

Scored from the asymmetric unit. A metal on a crystallographic symmetry axis is coordinated by two protomers while the deposition holds one, so the coordination number is a lower bound -- 9C8X reads CN 5 here and CN 10 in the biological assembly. Re-score the assembly before acting on anything short of a pass.

size_match.basis: La3+ Shannon effective radius 1.270 A at CN 10 (Shannon, R. D. (1976) Acta Crystallographica A32, 751-767, doi:10.1107/S0567739476001551) plus donor oxygen 1.40 A, the r(O2-) anchor of that scale, predicts a 2.670 A mean donor distance; observed 2.570 A, residual -0.100 A. Scaled by the 0.150 A width of the trivalent lanthanide series at CN 10.
size_match.caveat: Size propensity only: how well this ion's Shannon radius fits the observed donor distance at the observed coordination number. Not an affinity, not a binding constant, not a selectivity prediction. The whole La3+ -> Lu3+ contraction is ~0.18 A and adjacent lanthanides differ by ~0.01-0.02 A, which is at or below the coordinate error of a 2.0-2.5 A structure, so adjacent-pair differences in this number are not resolvable. The r(O2-) = 1.40 A anchor describes oxides, not protein carboxylate and carbonyl donors: over 279 sites at CN 8-9 in this project's corpus the prediction runs 0.045 A long, so no ion reaches a fit of 1.0 and the ranking between ions is sounder than any single value. Shannon tabulates only 3 of 15 trivalent lanthanides at CN 10, so the series width used as the denominator is a lower bound and this fit is correspondingly harsh.

target_coordination_fit.basis: Aqueous and solid-state coordination numbers for the trivalent rare earths (Greenwood & Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements): the larger ions are 9-coordinate as [Ln(H2O)9]3+ and the smaller ones 8-coordinate. Ca2+ is given its canonical protein geometry, CN 7 pentagonal bipyramidal.
target_coordination_fit.caveat: Whether a coordination number falls in an ion's usual range is a statement about geometry and nothing else. It is not an affinity, not a selectivity prediction, and not evidence that the ion was observed in this site. Neighbouring lanthanides share almost identical ranges, so a site compatible with one is compatible with several; this can rule a site in, never rule a competitor out. Descriptive, not a constraint. Ln3+ bonding is essentially electrostatic and non-directional, so coordination geometry is set by the ligands and a site outside this range is unusual rather than wrong. A coordination number read from an asymmetric unit is also a lower bound (see geometry.py), so a site reading below the minimum may simply be truncated.
target_coordination_fit.statement: CN 10 falls inside the range La3+ is normally found in (8-10).

size_match.caveat: Size propensity only: how well this ion's Shannon radius fits the observed donor distance at the observed coordination number. Not an affinity, not a binding constant, not a selectivity prediction. The whole La3+ -> Lu3+ contraction is ~0.18 A and adjacent lanthanides differ by ~0.01-0.02 A, which is at or below the coordinate error of a 2.0-2.5 A structure, so adjacent-pair differences in this number are not resolvable.
